newsitem.title: USA: American freed after Korean spy charges found dead.
newsitem.headline: American freed after Korean spy charges found dead.

text.p: Evan Hunziker, who was held in North Korea for three months on spying charges before being freed last month, was found dead on Wednesday, an apparent suicide, police said.
Hunziker, whose body was found in the basement lounge of his mother's Tacoma hotel, appeared to have died from a single gunshot wound to the head, police spokesman Jim Mattheis said.

"At this time no note has been found but it does appear to be a suicide," Mattheis said. He said the body was found about 6:30 a.m. PST (1430 GMT) by employees of the Olympus Motel, a residential hotel in downtown Tacoma owned by Hunziker's South Korean-born mother. A .357 calibre revolver was found nearby.

Hunziker, 26, had been living in the hotel since his return on Thanksgiving Day, Mattheis said. North Korean authorities freed him on Nov. 26, three months after he crossed into the Communist-ruled country from China and was detained on charges of spying and illegal entry.

The spying charges, believed to be the first against an American civilian since the Korean War, were denounced as outlandish by Hunziker's family and U.S. government officials, who suggested Pyongyang was using the young drifter as a pawn in a game of international diplomacy.

Hunziker claimed he crossed the Yalu River into North Korea to spread the gospel of Christianity after finding religion last year in an Alaska jail, where he was serving time on a drunk-driving conviction.

He spoke at least some Korean and had been to South Korea on two occasions but he was much larger than most Koreans and resembled his father of Swedish descent more than his mother, so he would have stood out in the closed North Korean society.
After he was apprehended by North Korean farmers on Aug. 24, Hunziker spent a month in a detention centre near the border before being moved to a hotel in Pyongyang.

U.S. Representative Bill Richardson, a New Mexico Democrat who secured his release and who is now U.S. ambassador-designate to the United Nations, described him at the time as "a confused young man, good intentions, very idealistic."

Evan Carl Hunziker was born in Tacoma but was raised in Alaska by his mother, Jong Nye Hunziker, after his parents divorced when he was 3. He returned to the Tacoma area for high school, where he wrestled and played football well enough to win a scholarship to a community college.
But he never graduated and ended up working on fishing boats in Alaska and doing odd jobs for his mother's hotel. He was married briefly to a woman he met in South Korea.
"He started doing drugs in college and he got himself into trouble," his father, Edwin, a Korean War veteran, told the Washington Post.
At the time of his return from North Korea, Hunziker was wanted in Alaska on several charges including assault and reckless driving.
Hunziker, who paid a $5,000 "hotel bill" on leaving North Korea, told reporters he had been treated humanely there.
